facts.headline: The world's most famous square was almost replaced by a glass tower
facts.body_html: In the 1990s, developers planned a glass tower next to Jemaa el-Fnaa, the square that flips from a daytime market into a spontaneous food and performance arena every night. Writer Juan Goytisolo's campaign against it got UNESCO to name the square's oral traditions a protected heritage in 2001 — the first designation of its kind.

facts.headline: A 14th-century school's tilework wasn't decoration — it was a lesson
facts.body_html: At Ben Youssef Madrasa, once the largest Islamic school in North Africa, every wall is covered in carved cedar, zellij tile and stucco arranged in complex geometric patterns built as a visual argument about the infinite — the mathematics was literally part of the curriculum.

facts.headline: This palace's 160 rooms were designed so no room would win
facts.body_html: Built for Grand Vizier Ba Ahmed, who effectively ruled Morocco while the sultan was a child, Bahia Palace's rooms were deliberately decorated so no single room outranked another — keeping his rival wives and concubines from claiming precedence. He died in 1900, and the sultan's men stripped the palace bare within hours.

facts.headline: This leather dye recipe hasn't changed in 900 years — pigeon droppings included
facts.body_html: Marrakech's leather tanners still soften hides in stone vats using pigeon droppings and quicklime, then color them with natural dyes like saffron and indigo — the same process used since the medieval era. The vats sit downwind on purpose; shopkeepers still hand visitors sprigs of mint for a reason.

facts.headline: A fashion designer bought this garden just to stop it from becoming a hotel
facts.body_html: French painter Jacques Majorelle spent 40 years building this garden and patented its vivid blue paint as "Majorelle Blue." After his death it fell into ruin — until Yves Saint Laurent bought it in 1980 to save it from demolition. His ashes are scattered here.

facts.headline: Builders tore down a finished mosque over a tiny alignment mistake
facts.body_html: When the original Koutoubia mosque was found slightly misaligned with Mecca, the Almohads didn't fix it — they built an entirely new one next door, completed in 1199. Its proportions became the template for Seville's Giralda and Rabat's Hassan Tower.

facts.headline: Legend says this entire palm forest grew from spat-out fruit pits
facts.body_html: The Palmeraie, Marrakech's palm grove oasis on the city's edge, is said by legend to have sprung from date pits spat out by marching Almoravid soldiers centuries ago. Barely visible from the medina, the oasis is still there today.
